Round One: Depends on where they are, and which characters they replace. If they replace some of the non-key staff, there's an excellent chance that many of them are eaten before the park owner invites the inspectors. If they replace the inspectors and children (everyone who goes out in the vehicles), they die by a large carnivorous dinosaur, at least assuming that in this universe they haven't seen the park because they're living it. If any of them replace the tech specialist, dinosaurs never happen because the computers can't deal with the lines of DNA. Alternatively, if they replace the tech specialist right at the start of the movie events, then everything goes on fine because the dinosaurs don't get out.

Round Two: Depends on how these individuals are housed, which DNA version of the band they are, and whether there is a tech specialist to sabotage everything. If these individuals are housed by member, such that all of the lead singers or all of the guitarists are in the same enclosure, then it is much less likely that there will be the sort of cohesion and teamwork that is shown in the band. If they are housed by group, such that each enclosure has a full band, perhaps told to perform a different song per enclosure, then some teamwork might be done. First things first, with instruments come instrument accessories. Guitar and microphone cables can be turned into rope if push comes to shove, and may be able to be used to create shorts in the electric fences to allow escape. Unfortunately for the band members, if they don't take out the cameras, they will quickly be discovered to not be in their cages since they can't reproduce (the cameras are pretty much only good at counting the number of individuals you expect).

Another point of contention is that probably not all of the band members are equal. There is the original band, who presumably is not a part of the park, and is the original DNA. In the book, because of the incompleteness of the DNA, there are different versions of the creatures, with each new version being a "more complete" batch of DNA. For example, the raptors are on Version 4.0. Given the amount of time it takes to create adult humans, there are probably many versions of the band in the park, ranging from newborns with the best DNA of the lot, to adults who are probably less capable. This is a major disadvantage for the band members.

Finally, Round Two belongs to the band, as the original group would force everyone off the island with a cease and desist.

Round Three: After the hullabaloo of Round Two, the band scientists have decided to do something extraordinary and not against any law yet. They have decided to take their current DNA batches and combine them with some dinosaur DNA. After a quick search, there are 6 members of the band. There were 6 major dinosaurs in the park. Let's match them up.

* Lead vocalist - T. rex (lead dinosaur, awesome roar)
* Drummer - Brachiosaurus (because they boom when they walk)
* Guitarist - Dilophosaurus
* Bassist - Gallimimus
* Electronics specialist - Triceratops
* Keyboardist - Velociraptor

With these combinations, weirdly enough, only the behavior came through, except for the guitarist-dinosaur hybrid who can spit poison. Honestly, I'm going to give this one to the band because a 40' tall lead vocalist with that sort of voice would probably drive everyone off on its own. Also, unless the caretakers prepare for the size of an 85' Brachiosaurus, those will be able to break the fences for everyone since these individuals still have enough human intelligence for music and strategy.

Round Four - Dinosaurs take it so hard.

Round Five - Normal raptors are going to be the real threat. The rest of the dinosaurs, except the Gallimimus, are probably taken out by their respective band members. If the raptors work together with the T. rex to take down the lead vocalist hybrid, then the dinosaurs will win by having the T. rex for other matchups. Best case for the band is if the big guys focus on the raptors, and maybe the T. rex, although I believe the lead vocalist hybrid can take the T. rex in a one-on-one. Probably 7/10 to dinosaurs.

Well, you have to remember that a popular social media platform was not invented in a bubble. Social networks have always been a thing in real life, and when people came online, those followed. Before the true social networking sites came online, you still had people connecting together via chat rooms and message boards. Email services had contact cards that you filled out with your contacts' information for the real world.

Eventually, websites that people actually call social networking websites started to appear. One was an early platform, but the big one was another site that allowed users to create personal pages and link to their friends' pages. It also had an embedded music player that was great for bands, so a lot of groups used it for promotion. The biggest complaints with that platform were that users had too much control over their profiles, often resulting in poorly designed pages with autoplaying media, and that it was misused by some individuals to target minors. A popular online resource has a decent writeup about that platform.

Another platform came along near the height of the previous site's popularity, but it focused initially on exclusivity, allowing only college students at select institutions to join. Over time, it lowered that barrier. Compared to the earlier site, this platform avoided user-caused interface issues by not allowing modifications to user profiles. Instead, users could fill out information about themselves in sections that still exist on the site today.
